findings.explanation: aws_iam_role_policy.codecommit is created when var.reponame != "", but its role attribute reads aws_iam_role.codebuild[count.index] — and that role is created only when var.role == "". Supply both a CodeCommit repo and your own IAM role, which are two independently documented options, and the policy exists while the role it indexes does not. Terraform errors with "Invalid index ... the collection has no elements" before it can plan anything. No attribute rule can see this: each resource's own count is valid, and the defect only exists in the relationship between two different count expressions. I reproduced it with a minimal two-resource config sharing the same shape and confirmed the plan-time failure. The intent is wrong as well as the index: if the caller brought their own role, the CodeCommit permissions should attach to that role, not to a role this module never created.
findings.remediation: Gate the policy on both conditions and attach to whichever role is actually in use. Change count to var.reponame == "" || var.role != "" ? 0 : 1 if the module should only manage permissions on roles it owns, or attach to data.aws_iam_role.existing when var.role is set. Either way the [count.index] must not index a differently-gated resource.
findings.title: Module fails at plan time whenever both role and reponame are supplied: codecommit policy indexes a role gated on a different condition

findings.explanation: The event pattern matches CodeCommit events whose resource ARN ends in ${var.name}, but aws_iam_role_policy.codecommit grants codecommit:GitPull and friends on ${var.reponame}. These are two different variables describing the same repository, and nothing forces them to agree — var.name is the build name and defaults to nothing in common with var.reponame. Whenever they differ the module is broken in one of two directions: the rule watches a repository that does not exist so builds never trigger, or it triggers on a repository the build role has no permission to clone. A rules engine compares attributes against constants, not two interpolations of different variables against each other for semantic equivalence.
findings.remediation: Use var.reponame in the event pattern's resource ARN, matching the IAM policy, since the rule only exists when var.reponame is set. Alternatively drop var.name from the trigger path entirely and derive both from one variable.
findings.title: CloudWatch Events rule watches the repository named var.name while the IAM policy grants access to var.reponame

findings.explanation: var.environment defaults image to aws/codebuild/nodejs:6.3.1. Node.js 6 reached end of life in April 2019 and receives no security patches, and the whole aws/codebuild/<language>:<version> curated image family has since been retired by AWS in favour of aws/codebuild/standard:N.0 and the amazonlinux2 images. Any caller who does not override var.environment therefore gets a build environment that is both unpatched and, in practice, no longer resolvable — so this is a live default, not a dormant one. HLD_AWS_095/096/097 all inspect this resource but none looks at the image, so nothing flagged it.
findings.remediation: Change the default image to a currently supported curated image, e.g. aws/codebuild/standard:7.0, and note in the variable description that the aws/codebuild/<language> family is retired.
findings.title: Default build image is a retired CodeBuild curated image carrying a Node.js runtime that reached EOL in 2019

findings.explanation: The role granted to the build holds codebuild:UpdateProject and codebuild:StartBuild scoped to aws_codebuild_project.build.arn — its own project. A build can therefore rewrite the project definition and start a new build under it. The sharpest consequence is privileged_mode: a build can set it to true and re-trigger itself, obtaining a privileged Docker container and, from there, escape to the build host. It can also repoint the buildspec, which makes the change persist for every later build rather than only the compromised one. Scoping the resource ARN, which is what the deterministic wildcard rules check, does not help here because the dangerous target is the project itself.
findings.remediation: Drop codebuild:UpdateProject unless a build genuinely needs to reconfigure its own project — StartBuild and StopBuild cover self-triggering. If it must stay, add a condition restricting it, and set privileged_mode explicitly on the resource so drift is visible.
findings.title: Build role can call codebuild:UpdateProject on its own project, letting a build rewrite the environment it runs in

findings.explanation: The confused-deputy condition uses ArnLike on arn:aws:events:<region>:<account>:rule/*, so any EventBridge rule in the account can assume this role and start the build. The rule this role exists for has a statically known name, codecommit-${var.name}, so the wildcard buys nothing. Naming it exactly does not create a dependency cycle, because the condition needs only the name string, not a reference to the rule resource. This is a self-review of a condition added earlier in this same session.
findings.remediation: Replace the rule/* wildcard with the specific rule name the role is created for.
findings.title: Trigger role trust policy scopes aws:SourceArn to every EventBridge rule in the account, though the rule name is statically known

findings.explanation: The statement grants ssm:GetParameters (plural) and ssm:PutParameter. The buildspec env.parameter-store block uses the plural GetParameters API so that path works, but any direct aws ssm get-parameter call in a build command hits the singular GetParameter action and is denied. Those are separate IAM actions, not aliases. This matters more now that the statement is scoped: previously the resource was "*" but the action list was the same, so the gap existed and was equally silent.
findings.remediation: Add ssm:GetParameter alongside ssm:GetParameters in the same statement.
findings.title: Build role can call ssm:GetParameters but not ssm:GetParameter, so a buildspec reading one parameter is denied

findings.explanation: var.sse_algorithm defaults to aws:kms while var.kms_key_id defaults to the empty string, and both feed aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration.artifacts. The result is SSE-KMS under the account's AWS-managed aws/s3 key rather than a customer-managed key, which means no key policy of your own gates decryption and the key cannot be disabled or audited independently. aws_codebuild_project.build.encryption_key takes the same empty default. The configuration reads as though a CMK is in play, which is the mismatch worth knowing about; HLD_AWS_064 covers the CodeBuild side of CMK use but the pairing of a KMS algorithm with an absent key is what makes this easy to miss.
findings.remediation: Either default sse_algorithm to AES256 so the posture is honest about being AWS-managed, or document clearly that kms_key_id must be supplied for the aws:kms default to mean a customer-managed key.
findings.title: Default encryption posture advertises KMS but resolves to the AWS-managed key

findings.explanation: logs_bucket is set to "logging-680235478471/codebuild/", embedding what appears to be a real 12-digit AWS account ID in a public repository. Account IDs are not secrets on their own, but they are useful to an attacker for cross-account role enumeration and for targeting S3 bucket names, and they should not ship in example code. It also makes the example non-functional for anyone else, since that bucket exists only in that account.
findings.remediation: Derive the bucket from data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id, which the example already declares, or take it as a variable with no default.
findings.title: Example hardcodes a real AWS account ID in the log bucket name

findings.explanation: When var.kms_key_id is set, it becomes both the S3 default-encryption key for the artifact bucket and aws_codebuild_project.build.encryption_key. The example does exactly this with a CMK whose key policy grants only the account root (EnableAccountRootAccess), which delegates access to IAM policies. But data.aws_iam_policy_document.codebuild contains no kms:* action at all, so the build role has no kms:GenerateDataKey, kms:Decrypt or kms:Encrypt on the key. CodeBuild documents that its service role needs those on the project's CMK, and S3 PutObject into an SSE-KMS bucket needs kms:GenerateDataKey; builds fail with AccessDenied when encrypting artifacts, or on encrypted cache and source. Nothing is flagged because each resource is individually valid: the gap is between the variable, the key policy in the caller, and the role policy in this module.
findings.remediation: Add a conditional statement (dynamic block when var.kms_key_id != "") granting kms:Decrypt, kms:Encrypt, kms:ReEncrypt*, kms:GenerateDataKey* and kms:DescribeKey on the supplied key, resolving a bare key id to an ARN. Not auto-fixable: the key may be an alias, id or ARN and the correct resource form depends on which the caller supplies.
findings.title: Build role has no KMS permissions, so supplying kms_key_id breaks builds writing to the SSE-KMS artifact bucket

confirmed_safe: HLD_AWS_292 — the KMS principal is an account-root ARN, not a wildcard
still_unresolvable: HLD_AWS_308 — the log target bucket comes from var.logs_bucket and lives outside the configuration
